safety.alert: Concentrated clove oil can burn tissue; swallowing amounts can cause severe liver injury, especially in children; allergy possible.
Essential oil can irritate mucosa/skin; do not assume undiluted oil is safe to ingest.
Concentrated essential oil and camphor can cause seizures/poisoning; caution pregnancy and children.
Can worsen reflux; concentrates can irritate; high pulegone exposure is unsafe.
Cassia substitutions can have much higher coumarin and liver risk; oil can irritate.
Some concentrated high-bioavailability curcumin products linked to liver injury; pregnancy/medication cautions.
High-intake supplements may aggravate reflux and interact with medicines.
Bleeding interaction concerns and surgery precautions; raw topical garlic can severely burn skin.
Extracts are riskier than customary brewed tea; sleep, drug and iron-absorption cautions.
Piperine concentrates can raise exposure to some medicines; culinary black pepper is not equivalent to concentrated extract.
Oil/supplements may interact with diabetes/blood-pressure medications; allergic reactions.
Concentrated extracts may affect glucose/clotting and interact with medication; pregnancy caution.
Medication interactions possible, including anticoagulants and diabetes drugs; insomnia possible.
Rare liver injury reports, thyroid effects, pregnancy caution; product quality matters.
Nausea/diarrhea and possible drug interactions; pregnancy safety unestablished.
Rare liver injury with some preparations reported; ensure species/authenticity.
High amounts can be toxic; pregnancy and medication cautions; counterfeiting common.
May cause sleepiness or interact with sedatives/thyroid medication; essential oil not equivalent to tea.
Potential sedation/drug interaction; do not infer potent MAOI effects from trace disputed alkaloid reports.
Serious hypertension, edema, low potassium, arrhythmia; risks with diuretics, digoxin, heart/kidney disease and pregnancy.
GI upset and interaction potential; do not equate frankincense aroma oil with boswellic acid extract.
Leaf food use differs from concentrated root/bark products; pregnancy and quality cautions.
Do not use herbal preparations for malaria in place of approved ACT; resistance and variable dosing are major dangers.
Sleep disruption, palpitations and anxiety; pregnancy and medication cautions.
Allergy and GI reactions possible; do not assume pure erinacine content in fruiting-body supplements.
Possible bleeding interactions and liver problems with some extracts; taxonomic mislabeling common.
Immunologic effects may matter with autoimmune conditions/immunosuppressants; quality and species checks.
Raw/undercooked shiitake can cause shiitake dermatitis; fungal allergies.
Mushroom allergy; potential interactions with diabetes drugs/anticoagulants.
Allergy, product contamination/mislabelling, potential medication interactions.
Food allergy possible; always cook; substrate affects metal/contaminant content.
High oxalate exposure has caused oxalate kidney injury, including severe renal failure; especially concerning with kidney disease/stones.
Essential-oil products differ from tea; reflux, indigestion; avoid application near infant face.
Enhanced-absorption curcumin products have reported liver injury; drug interactions require review.
Supplements may increase bleeding risk; raw topical garlic may burn skin.
Rare supplement-associated liver injury and thyroid/other medication interactions.
Licorice glycyrrhizin can cause dangerous cardiovascular and potassium effects.
Artemisia plant material not recommended for malaria by WHO; delay of effective treatment can be life-threatening.
Published case report of oxalate kidney injury associated with chronic chaga powder ingestion.
Cassia and Ceylon are chemically different; prolonged cassia coumarin exposure can be risky.
Culinary rhizome use is not equivalent to concentrated panduratin A; no validated human antiviral dose or treatment safety. Cell cytotoxicity measured in the Thai study.
Food use involves identified, appropriately handled edible galls; laboratory or agricultural smut cultures are not automatically food-safe. Composition depends on maize and harvest stage.

cultural_uses.reported_use: Historically cultivated and traded from Maluku; dried buds are used as a flavorful culinary spice.
cultural_uses.limitations: Culinary use is not evidence of treatment or safety of concentrated clove oil.

cultural_uses.reported_use: Kew documents long traditional use for dental discomfort and digestive complaints across several regions.
cultural_uses.limitations: Regional use is documented broadly; a particular preparation cannot be attributed to a named community from this source.

cultural_uses.reported_use: Historical Indian medicinal applications include digestion, topical skin care, and inflammation.
cultural_uses.limitations: Turmeric culinary rhizome, topical paste and concentrated curcumin capsules are chemically and clinically different.

cultural_uses.reported_use: Kew records turmeric in wedding rituals and the Holi festival, as well as cooking and dyeing.
cultural_uses.limitations: This is cultural use, not a claim of measurable biological benefit.

cultural_uses.reported_use: Traditional applications include liver disorders, dysentery, ulcers and inflammation.
cultural_uses.limitations: These are descriptions of traditional indications, not evidence turmeric cures dysentery or liver disease.

cultural_uses.reported_use: Kew reports turmeric used historically to support digestion and for inflammation-related complaints.
cultural_uses.limitations: Different Curcuma species have overlapping common names in Chinese medicine; verify botanical identity.

cultural_uses.reported_use: Kew documents use of ginger in folk medicines in India and Burma (Myanmar); the cited page does not enumerate region-specific indications.
cultural_uses.limitations: Do not infer a specific use or dose from this broad ethnobotanical mention.

cultural_uses.reported_use: Kew documents medicinal use in Ecuador and Mexico, without detailing particular uses by named communities.
cultural_uses.limitations: No community-level attribution or condition is verified by this source.

cultural_uses.reported_use: Flora of Iraq records leaves applied as poultices on tumors and ulcers.
cultural_uses.limitations: Historical poultice use must not be read as evidence of cancer treatment or safe application to open skin.

cultural_uses.reported_use: Flora of Oman records traditional use of pounded leaves for burns and sunburn.
cultural_uses.limitations: This record does not establish safety or benefit on burns; burns require proper first aid.

cultural_uses.tradition: Flora of Tropical East Africa: recorded practices
cultural_uses.reported_use: Regional ethnobotanical accounts include stomach complaints, intestinal worms and coughs.
cultural_uses.limitations: Multiple local traditions are grouped by the Flora source; exact community and formulation must be verified before finer attribution.

cultural_uses.reported_use: A 2022 systematic narrative review documents traditional applications for intestinal worms and sores or skin infections in Africa and South Asia.
cultural_uses.limitations: The review summarizes heterogeneous traditions; do not assume the same preparation or that treatment is effective.

cultural_uses.reported_use: A literature review documents long-standing traditional applications for digestion, appetite, pain, and skin complaints.
cultural_uses.limitations: The review includes many preclinical claims; this record is solely about historically reported use.

cultural_uses.preparation: Fresh, dried white or processed red root
cultural_uses.reported_use: Ginseng has a traditional role as a calming agent and in practices associated with supporting resilience to stress.
cultural_uses.limitations: “Adaptogen” is a traditional/functional label, not a quantified clinical effect.

cultural_uses.reported_use: The preparation of Asian ginseng into white and red ginseng represents distinct processing traditions and produces differing preparations.
cultural_uses.limitations: No clinical equivalence between the red and white products is implied.

cultural_uses.tradition: Traditional Chinese Medicine / historical materia medica
cultural_uses.reported_use: Classical Chinese sources associate lingzhi with replenishing qi, calming the mind, and relieving cough-related complaints.
cultural_uses.limitations: The commercial name “reishi” can cover several Ganoderma species; do not assume all species share chemical composition or clinical effects.

cultural_uses.reported_use: Lingzhi has historical symbolism related to longevity and auspiciousness in Chinese art and Taoist culture.
cultural_uses.limitations: A symbolic association is not a longevity or efficacy claim.

cultural_uses.reported_use: Iranian scholars studying Avicenna and major Islamic medical texts report traditional indications for low mood and sleep.
cultural_uses.limitations: This is a reconstruction from historical sources, separate from modern clinical trials.

cultural_uses.tradition: Razi and broader Islamic traditional medicine
cultural_uses.reported_use: A source-based survey of Islamic medicine texts reports historical uses for pain, inflammation, and breathing complaints.
cultural_uses.limitations: Modern human efficacy depends on specific outcomes and preparations; this record is historical.

cultural_uses.preparation: Herbal leaf tea / oral leaf preparations
cultural_uses.reported_use: The EMA monograph recognizes relief of indigestion and flatulence on the basis of long-standing traditional use.
cultural_uses.limitations: EMA classifies peppermint LEAF evidence as traditional, distinct from peppermint OIL.

cultural_uses.reported_use: EMA describes evidence-supported use of certain peppermint OIL preparations for minor abdominal spasms, bloating and IBS-related discomfort.
cultural_uses.limitations: The evidence is for specified medicinal oil preparations, not homemade tea or undiluted essential oil.

cultural_uses.preparation: Inhaled or diluted topical medicinal oil
cultural_uses.reported_use: EMA recognizes cold/cough symptom relief and certain topical applications on the basis of traditional use, not the same clinical-evidence status as gut oil.
cultural_uses.limitations: Age and application-specific contraindications apply; concentrated essential oil can cause toxicity.

cultural_uses.tradition: Thai culinary and publicly documented herbal uses
cultural_uses.preparation: Culinary ingredient, distinct from purified chemical
cultural_uses.reported_use: Fingerroot is used as a regional culinary aromatic; pharmacological study discusses established culinary use.
cultural_uses.limitations: The paper documents broad culinary context, not a specific community practice or antiviral clinical benefit.

cultural_uses.reported_use: Traditionally valued as a food and condiment in Mexican gastronomy.
cultural_uses.limitations: Public culinary record only; no medicinal efficacy claim or restricted knowledge.

structures.scope: specific stereochemically defined small molecule; 2D via authoritative CID
structures.binding_warning: Structure and cell inhibition do not prove direct binding, human antiviral efficacy, or safe exposure.

binding.evidence_tier: direct structural and functional experiments, not human clinical outcome
binding.method: cryo-EM menthol-occupied pocket; functional electrophysiology; earlier mutational and computational analysis
binding.limitations: Do not extrapolate these pocket contacts to any other phytochemical or species without experiments.

binding.evidence_tier: experimental protein–ligand structural evidence plus pharmacology
binding.method: x-ray structure in complex with caffeine (PDB 5MZP); broader pharmacology supported by human effects
binding.limitations: Other adenosine subtypes also implicated; dose and exposure determine relevance. Do not infer exact in-human affinity from structural diagram.

binding.effect_on_target: selective agonist activity in preclinical studies
binding.evidence_tier: preclinical receptor evidence; no validated compound-specific clinical benefit from clove
binding.method: receptor-binding and functional assays; mouse model
binding.limitations: This is not proof that clove essential oil achieves biologically relevant CB2 exposure, nor that combined clove constituents are synergistic.
